identity.notes: The local name carries a per-unit suffix and is the better key. The address is an nRF52 random-static address in all likelihood (the SDK derives a per-unit bootloader name from its last two bytes), stable across reboots but not hardware-confirmed.

methods.notes: Prefix match on the local name, as the vendor SDK does. The sensor service UUID (64a70011-f691-4b93-a6f4-0968f5b648f8) is not known to be advertised, so the name is the only pre-connection signal.

identification.notes: The vendor SDK identifies a wand by local name alone: anything whose advertised name starts with "Kano-Wand". The full name is reported as "Kano-Wand-75-XX-XX" (Hackaday project 161832; the SDK's own demos search for "Kano-Wand-75"); the two trailing groups are probably the last two bytes of the BLE address, by analogy with the SDK's bootloader naming, but that is unconfirmed. No advertised service UUID or manufacturer data is documented. Kano holds Bluetooth company ID 0x07d4 and MA-M block 18:74:e2:8; whether the wand uses either is not established, so neither is a matcher here.

device.manufacturer: Kano Computing Limited (London; in administration since 2023-06-06)
device.name: Kano Harry Potter Coding Kit Wand
device.notes:
The wand from Kano's 2018 Harry Potter Coding Kit: a Nordic nRF52832 (SoftDevice S132) with a 9-axis IMU (accelerometer, gyroscope, magnetometer), one push button, a vibration motor and an RGB LED, powered by two AAA cells. It talks BLE GATT directly to the tablet or computer running the Kano app; there is no hub and no cloud in the control path. The wand streams its orientation as a quaternion, reports button presses, and takes LED colour and vibration-pattern writes. The Kano app did the rest — turning the orientation stream into on-screen "spells" — on the host, so gesture recognition is out of scope here: this spec makes the wand a gesture-input device and stops there.
Why it is here: Kano Computing Limited entered administration on 2023-06-06 (The Gazette, notice 4374009; Companies House 08375450). In January 2023 TechCrunch reported Kano was no longer actively marketing the wand, and retailers list the kit as discontinued. The companion app's last iPad release is 1.3.11 (2021-02-06), still listed as of 2026-10. A phone-direct BLE device whose vendor is insolvent and whose app has not been updated in five years is the case this registry exists for.
The vendor published an SDK for the wand under MIT (@kano/devices-sdk on npm, October 2018), so the GATT layout and byte formats below are the vendor's own statement, not a reconstruction; see openness. The LED boot animation plays at power-up and may override an early colour write. The wand disconnects on its own after inactivity without any notification; the SDK writes a keep-alive byte to hold it.

openness.notes: Kano published @kano/devices-sdk (MIT, author "Kano Computing") on npm in 2018: a platform-independent JavaScript SDK whose wand module names every service and characteristic and encodes every write. That makes this a vendor-documented interface in all but prose; the SDK's GitHub repository has since vanished (404), so the npm tarball is the surviving copy. Units and scaling of the sensor values are NOT stated by the SDK (it emits raw integers) and come from the hobby clients.

exclusivity.recovery: Close the Kano app (or whichever client holds the wand), or pull a battery for a moment, then connect.

pairing.notes: No link-layer pairing, no bonding, no application-layer handshake: the vendor SDK and all three hobby clients connect with no security parameters and read and write every characteristic on a bare connection. One central at a time is the ordinary BLE peripheral limit, assumed rather than observed.

credentials.notes: No secrets anywhere: open GATT, no PIN, no bond, no account.

factory_reset.description: The build book's troubleshooting is limited to battery polarity, the wake button and four help codes (WA2 power, WA3 connection, WA4 app, WA5 unsupported device) for the vendor help site, which is gone. In practice "pull the batteries" is the reset.
factory_reset.effect: No reset procedure is documented. The wand stores no pairing, no credentials and no owner; the only state a reset could touch is the magnetometer calibration, and whether that persists across a battery change is not known.

methods.description: Scan for a "Kano-Wand" name, connect, enable notifications on the button and quaternion characteristics, write the orientation reset once, then write the keep-alive byte periodically so the wand does not sleep. Button presses and the orientation stream then arrive as notifications; LED colour and vibration are plain writes.
methods.name: Connect and subscribe

steps.action: Fit two AAA cells. The blue LED on the board should light; if not, check battery polarity.
steps.expect: Blue LED on; it flashes while the wand searches for a connection.

steps.action: If the wand is dark, press its button once to wake it. Close the Kano app if it is running — the wand holds one connection.
Scan for a local name starting Kano-Wand and connect.
steps.expect: The blue LED stops flashing and stays on.

steps.action: Write 01 to 64a70004-f691-4b93-a6f4-0968f5b648f8 so the orientation stream is zeroed to the wand's current pose.
steps.expect: Eight-byte quaternion notifications begin; the button characteristic notifies 01 on press and 00 on release.

steps.action: Write 01 to 64a7000f-f691-4b93-a6f4-0968f5b648f8 periodically to keep the wand awake; it otherwise disconnects after inactivity without notice.

setup.notes: Nothing to provision: fit two AAA cells, press the button to wake the wand, connect, subscribe. The build book says the blue Bluetooth LED flashes while the wand is looking for a connection and goes steady once connected. No account, no cloud, no bond. The vendor SDK is a working open implementation of exactly this, which is where the medium confidence comes from; this project has not run it.

rejoin.notes: BLE-only; there is no network to rejoin. Any central may connect once the current one has disconnected or the wand has timed out.

testing.notes: Not driven against hardware by this project. Every UUID and byte layout below is read from the vendor's own published SDK (@kano/devices-sdk 1.0.1, MIT) and cross-checked against three independent hobby clients; nothing has been replayed on a wand.

entities.name: Button
entities.notes: A level, not an event: 01 on press, 00 on release.

entities.name: Orientation W
entities.notes: Quaternion component, -1..1, relative to the last reset_orientation.

entities.name: Battery Status
entities.notes: Raw byte; not declared as a battery percentage until its scale is checked.

entities.name: Temperature Raw
entities.notes: Raw int16; unit and scale unknown.

entities.name: LED
entities.notes: set_color is deliberately unbound: the LED takes a packed RGB565 word (set_led's rgb565 parameter) and the command vocabulary has no way to say "pack three channels into one big-endian uint16". A consumer that implements the packing in protocol_details.rgb565 can drive set_led directly.

entities.name: Calibrate Magnetometer
entities.notes: Watch 64a70021-f691-4b93-a6f4-0968f5b648f8 for 02 (done) or 03 (failed); the orientation stream should be paused meanwhile.

evidence.documentation_review: Read on 2026-10-11: @kano/devices-sdk 1.0.1 from npm (wand, dfu, devices and platform modules, the demos and README); GammaGames/ kano_wand (module, wiki, FAQ); anzellai/wandkit's Go source; wizofe/ bluewand-python's README and scanner; sabas1080/KanoWandHack's Arduino sketch and Hackaday page and logs; Nordic's 2018-10-09 press release; Kano's build book PDF; The Gazette notice 4374009; Companies House 08375450 insolvency page; TechCrunch 2023-01-12 and 2023-01-27; the App Store listing for the Kano Code / Harry Potter Wand Kit app. All five code sources agree on every UUID; the vendor SDK is the only one that encodes every write and decodes every read, and it is the basis for each byte layout above.
evidence.open_questions: Quaternion byte order and sign on hardware (vendor SDK vs Python client); the inactivity timeout and whether keep-alive extends it; battery and temperature scaling; whether Kano's bootloader enforces signed images and where images came from; the raw and motion characteristic layouts; whether the wand advertises any service UUID; what the "75" and the two trailing groups in the local name encode.

dfu_mode.notes: The vendor SDK names the bootloader "DFU-XX-XX" — "DFU-" plus the last two bytes of the wand's address, hyphenated, in whatever case the host printed them — and then scans for that exact name. A bootloader entered any other way would advertise the stack default "DfuTarg". Address behaviour is not observed; a stock nRF5 SDK bootloader without bond sharing would advertise at address+1, which is why the SDK matches on name rather than address.

enter.notes: The stack's buttonless characteristic 8ec90003 without bond sharing, preceded by the stack's set-name opcode (vendor SDK sequence: set name, wait ~100 ms, write 01, wait for disconnect).

image.format: nrfutil DFU zip: manifest.json whose application entry names a .dat init packet and a .bin image (vendor SDK loads these two).
image.notes: Secure DFU bootloaders verify an ECDSA P-256 signature in the init packet by default, and the vendor SDK's error table includes the stack's "init packet does not contain a signature" code, but whether Kano's bootloader actually enforces signing has not been established. Where the Kano app obtained images is unknown; no public URL is known, and the Python client's author deliberately omitted updates to avoid bricking wands.

dfu.notes: From the vendor SDK's DFU module, which transcribes Nordic's Secure DFU client: packet-receipt notifications every 15 packets, 20-byte packets, select/create/calculate-checksum/execute per object with CRC32 checks, the init object first and the application image second. Nothing device-specific beyond the bootloader name was found. Not hardware-verified.

recovery.notes: The nRF5 SDK bootloader defaults (dual-bank where flash allows, 120 s inactivity timeout back to a valid application) are likely on an nRF52832 but have not been checked on a wand.

QuaternionNotification.description: One notification on 64a70002-f691-4b93-a6f4-0968f5b648f8: four int16 LE, order w x y z, each component x 1000.
parse_rules: Accept only eight-byte notifications; the Go client uses the length to tell this stream from the one-byte button notifications on a shared handler.
Constructed worked example (not a capture): e8 03 00 00 00 00 00 00 is w = 1.000, x = y = z = 0 — the identity pose right after reset_orientation. 18 fc 00 00 00 00 00 00 is w = -1.000.

dfu_sequence.bootloader_name: DFU-<addr byte 4>-<addr byte 5>, as the host prints the address (e.g. DFU-ee-ff)
dfu_sequence.entry: write 02 <len> <name> to 8ec90003, wait ~100 ms, write 01; the wand disconnects
dfu_sequence.source: @kano/devices-sdk lib/dfu.js — Nordic's documented Secure DFU procedure, nothing Kano-specific except the name
dfu_sequence.transfer: Subscribe to control point 8ec90001; set packet-receipt notifications to every 15 packets (02 0f 00); for the init packet then the image: select (06 01 / 06 02), create (01 01 / 01 02 with a LE uint32 length), stream 20-byte packets to 8ec90002, calculate checksum (03) and compare CRC32, execute (04). Responses are 60 <op> <result>; result 01 is success, 0b carries an extended error byte.

host_side_gesture_recognition.note: Spell recognition ran in the Kano app on the host, fed by this quaternion stream and the button. It is not a device protocol and is not documented here. The GammaGames demos show the stream is enough to drive a cursor or feed a direction-sequence gesture recogniser.

info_values_reported.basis: Values served by sabas1080/KanoWandHack's Arduino emulator, which the Kano desktop app detected (Hackaday log, 2018-12-09). They are what a 2018 wand plausibly returned, not a reading from one.

quaternion_stream.client_disagreement: The Python client decodes little-endian but labels the words y, -x, -w, z (a remap to its own screen axes); the Go client decodes big-endian unsigned w, x, y, z and never got a usable mapping out of it (its own FIXME). The vendor SDK's little-endian signed w, x, y, z is declared. Confirming on hardware is the top open item.
quaternion_stream.layout: 8 bytes: int16 LE w, x, y, z; component = raw / 1000

rgb565.note: The same formula appears in the vendor SDK and the Python client (which credits the SDK). Only the top 5/6/5 bits of each channel survive, so a colour read back through any other path will not round-trip.
rgb565.packing: rgb565 = ((r & 0xf8) << 8) | ((g & 0xfc) << 3) | ((b & 0xf8) >> 3); sent as two bytes, high byte first, after the on/off byte

remaining_unknowns: Quaternion decode has not been checked on a wand: the vendor SDK (int16 LE, w x y z) is declared; the Python client remaps and negates, the Go client reads big-endian. One capture settles it.
The inactivity timeout, and whether writing 01 to the keep-alive characteristic actually extends it (the vendor SDK does it; the Python client's author doubted it).
Battery status scaling (one byte; reads of 0 reported) and temperature unit/scale (int16 LE, raw).
Whether the Secure DFU bootloader enforces signatures, where firmware images came from, the bootloader's address behaviour and inactivity timeout — none observed.
Layouts of the raw (64a7000a-f691-4b93-a6f4-0968f5b648f8) and motion (64a7000c-f691-4b93-a6f4-0968f5b648f8) characteristics; nothing reads them.
Whether any service UUID or manufacturer data (Kano company ID 0x07d4) is advertised; the vendor SDK matches on the local name alone.
The local-name suffix: 'Kano-Wand-75-XX-XX' is reported; whether 75 is a model code and XX-XX the address tail is a guess.
Whether a factory reset exists and whether magnetometer calibration persists across a battery change.

format.name: organisation
format.notes: Variable length — 20 is the longest a default-MTU read returns, not a fixed width.

characteristics.name: Organisation
characteristics.notes: UTF-8 string, variable length; the whole read is the value.

format.name: software_version
format.notes: Variable length — 20 is the longest a default-MTU read returns, not a fixed width.

characteristics.name: Software version
characteristics.notes: UTF-8 version string of the wand firmware, e.g. a dotted triple.

characteristics.name: Hardware build
characteristics.notes: The vendor SDK takes byte 0 as the hardware build number. The Python client decodes it as a string instead; the SDK's reading is the one declared here.

services.name: Wand information service
services.notes: Three read-only identity values. The vendor SDK reads organisation and software version as UTF-8 strings and the hardware build as a single byte. An Arduino emulator that the Kano desktop app recognised served "Kano Computing", "1.0.4" and 3 respectively; those are the emulator's values, not a reading from a wand.

format.name: battery_status
format.notes: Unit and scaling not established; probably a percentage, but reads of 0 have been reported.

characteristics.name: Battery status
characteristics.notes: One byte. The vendor SDK surfaces it as "battery status" with no unit; the Python client's author reports reads returning 0. Until someone checks it against a meter, treat it as an unscaled raw value rather than a percentage.

characteristics.name: User button
characteristics.notes: Notifies on every change: 01 when the button goes down, 00 when it is released. A read returns the current level.

vibrate.description: Play a vibration pattern. One byte, 1-7; the names are the Python client's (the vendor SDK passes a bare number). 1 is what the vendor SDK's own feature test sends.

characteristics.name: Vibration motor
characteristics.notes: Write one byte: a pattern number. The vendor SDK passes the number through untyped; the Python client names 1-7. What each pattern feels like, and whether values above 7 do anything, is not documented. A read returns the last pattern byte.

led_off.description: LED off: 00 00 00 (the vendor SDK sends a zero colour with the off state).

set_led.description: Set the LED on or off with a colour. state is 1 (on) or 0 (off); rgb565 is the packed colour, big-endian. A generic colour picker has to pack RGB888 into RGB565 first (protocol_details.rgb565), so this command is declared with the packed word rather than three channel bytes.

characteristics.name: LED
characteristics.notes: Three bytes: [on/off, colour high byte, colour low byte]. The colour is 16-bit RGB565 — red in the top five bits, green in the middle six, blue in the low five — sent high byte first. Pure red is 01 f8 00, pure green 01 07 e0, pure blue 01 00 1f, white 01 ff ff; the packing is in protocol_details.rgb565 with worked vectors. A read returns byte 0 (the on/off state) per the vendor SDK. The power-on boot animation can mask a colour written in the first moments after battery insertion.

characteristics.name: Keep-alive
characteristics.notes: Write 01 periodically to stop the wand sleeping. The vendor SDK exposes exactly this write; the Python client's author doubted it works. The inactivity timeout itself is not documented, and the wand gives no notification when it drops the link.

services.name: Wand IO service
services.notes: Button, battery, vibration motor, LED and keep-alive. The vendor SDK's Node platform writes without response wherever the characteristic allows it and with response otherwise; the Python client writes vibration, LED and keep-alive with response. Either works.

characteristics.name: Quaternions
characteristics.notes: Eight bytes per notification: four signed 16-bit little-endian integers in the order w, x, y, z (vendor SDK). Each is the quaternion component times 1000, so the range is -1000..1000 (reported independently by three clients). The frame is relative to whatever pose the wand had when the orientation reset was last written. The Python client reads the same bytes in a different order and negates two of them to suit its own axes, and the Go client reads them big-endian; both are client-side choices, and the vendor SDK's reading is the one declared here. No notification rate is documented. Streams whether or not the button is held.

reset_orientation.description: Zero the orientation stream to the wand's current pose: write 01.

characteristics.name: Quaternion reset
characteristics.notes: Write 01 to re-zero the orientation stream to the current pose. Clients do it once right after subscribing.

calibrate_magnetometer.description: Start a magnetometer calibration: write 01, then watch the notifications for 02 (done) or 03 (failed).

characteristics.name: Magnetometer calibration
characteristics.notes: Write 01 to start a magnetometer calibration; the characteristic then notifies a status byte, 02 when calibration has succeeded and 03 when it failed (vendor SDK). The SDK unsubscribes from the quaternion stream for the duration and resubscribes afterwards. What the user must do with the wand during calibration is not documented.

characteristics.name: Temperature
characteristics.notes: A signed 16-bit little-endian value (vendor SDK). Unit and scaling are not stated anywhere; most likely the IMU's die temperature. Declared raw until someone compares it with a thermometer.

characteristics.name: Raw sensor data
characteristics.notes: Named by the vendor SDK, used by nothing. Presumably the raw 9-axis samples; layout unknown. Properties are the emulator's, not confirmed.

characteristics.name: Motion
characteristics.notes: Named by the vendor SDK, used by nothing. Layout unknown. Properties are the emulator's, not confirmed.

services.name: Wand sensor service
services.notes: The orientation stream and its controls, plus a temperature. Two further characteristics (raw and motion) are named by the vendor SDK and never used by it or by any client; their layouts are unknown.

enter_bootloader.advanced_reason: Leaves the wand in its bootloader with no application controls until a valid image is transferred or the bootloader's inactivity timeout boots the old application (the nRF5 SDK default is 120 s; not confirmed on this wand). Have the vendor's DFU zip and a working DFU client ready before sending it.
enter_bootloader.description: Reboot into the Nordic Secure DFU bootloader: write 01. The wand disconnects and reappears under the name set with set_bootloader_name (or the stack default DfuTarg if none was set), expecting an init packet and image.

set_bootloader_name.advanced_reason: Sets the name the bootloader will advertise on the next bootloader entry. Nothing breaks, but it changes how the wand appears mid-update, so send it only as the first half of a deliberate firmware update.
set_bootloader_name.description: Tell the bootloader what to advertise as: 02, a length byte, then that many ASCII bytes. The vendor SDK uses "DFU-" plus the last two bytes of the wand's address as printed, e.g. DFU-ee-ff for aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff. Harmless on its own, but it exists only to precede enter_bootloader.

name.description: ASCII name the bootloader will advertise.

name_length.description: Byte length of name; must equal the number of bytes in name.

characteristics.name: Buttonless DFU (no bond sharing)
characteristics.notes: The stack's standard buttonless characteristic. The vendor SDK first writes opcode 02 with a name so the bootloader advertises as "DFU-XX-XX" (the last two address bytes, hex, hyphenated), waits about 100 ms, then writes opcode 01; the wand resets into the bootloader and the link drops. Responses arrive as indications beginning 20.

services.name: Nordic Secure DFU service
services.notes: Present in the running application for buttonless bootloader entry (vendor SDK). In the application only the buttonless characteristic is used; the control-point and packet characteristics (8ec90001-f315-4f60-9fb8-838830daea50 and 8ec90002-f315-4f60-9fb8-838830daea50) belong to the bootloader, which the SDK reconnects to under a name it set first. A GATT explorer lists this service read-only; see features.
